abstract: Centromeres direct chromosome segregation and are defined not by DNA sequence but by CENP-A-containing chromatin, raising the question of how centromeric identity is faithfully transmitted through DNA replication, and whether this process influences stem cell behavior. In the Drosophila male germline, germline stem cells (GSCs) assemble asymmetric sister centromeres linked to non-random sister-chromatid segregation, but how this asymmetry is established and whether it contributes to germline function remain unclear. Using high-resolution microscopy on cell-type and stage-specific chromatin fibers, we show that pre-existing CENP-A (CID in flies) is recycled asymmetrically onto newly replicated sister centromeres in early germ cells including GSCs, while differentiating progenitors redistribute CID nearly symmetrically. Inner kinetochore component CENP-C shows a similar pattern, with both proteins enriched on the lagging strand. The CID chaperone CAL1 associates with centromeres during S phase and is required for this asymmetric incorporation of both CID and CENP-C and for normal germline function; compromising CAL1 leads to either early-germline tumors or germ cell loss. Intriguingly, reducing lagging-strand Primase 1, a component of the DNA polymerase  (Pol) complex, is sufficient to induce sister centromere asymmetry in differentiating progenitors, promoting a stem cell-like centromere state, proper centrosome orientation, and niche-directed microtubule behavior during dedifferentiation of progenitors. Combining modest CID overexpression with Primase 1 reduction further enhances dedifferentiation and redifferentiation, significantly improving male fertility during aging and regeneration following {gamma}-irradiation. Together, these findings identify that replication-coupled, strand-biased centromere inheritance can be tuned to regulate cellular plasticity, linking DNA replication to regenerative capacity and reproductive fitness.
